parts.label: Part 2
parts.title: Future Food Supply
parts.subtitle: Climate change and new diseases threaten the limited varieties of seeds we depend on for food. Luckily, we still have many of the seeds used in the past—but we must take steps to save them.
parts.article:
Future Food Supply

A Six miles outside the town of Decorah, Iowa in the USA, an 890-acre stretch of rolling fields and woods called Heritage Farm is letting its crops go to seed. Everything about Heritage Farm is in stark contrast to the surrounding acres of intensively farmed fields of corn and soybean that are typical of modern agriculture. Heritage Farm is devoted to collecting rather than growing seeds. It is home to the Seed Savers Exchange, one of the largest non government-owned seed banks in the United States.

B In 1975 Diane Ott Whealy was given the seedlings of two plant varieties that her great grandfather had brought to America from Bavaria in 1870: Grandpa Ott’s morning glory and his German Pink tomato. Wanting to preserve similar traditional varieties, known as heirloom plants, Diane and her husband, Kent, decided to establish a place where the seeds of the past could be kept and traded. The exchange now has more than 13,000 members, and the many thousands of heirloom varieties they have donated are kept in its walk-in coolers, freezers, and root cellars. As you walk around an old red barn that is covered in Grandpa Ott’s beautiful morning glory blossoms, you come across the different vegetables, herbs, and flowers they have planted there.

C “Each year our members list their seeds in this,” Diane Ott Whealy says, handing over a copy of the Seed Savers Exchange 2010 Yearbook. It is as thick as a big-city telephone directory, with page after page of exotic beans, garlic, potatoes, peppers, apples, pears, and plums—each with its own name and personal history. For example, there’s an Estonian Yellow Cherry tomato, which was brought to the seed bank by “an elderly Russian lady” who lived in Tallinn, and a Persian Star garlic from “a bazaar in Samarkand.” There’s also a bean donated by archaeologists searching for pygmy elephant fossils in New Mexico.

D Heirloom vegetables have become fashionable in the United States and Europe over the past decade, prized by a food movement that emphasizes eating locally and preserving the flavor and uniqueness of heirloom varieties. Found mostly in farmers' markets and boutique groceries, heirloom varieties have been squeezed out of supermarkets in favor of modern single-variety fruits and vegetables bred to ship well and have a uniform appearance, not to enhance flavor. But the movement to preserve heirloom varieties goes way beyond the current interest in North America and Europe in tasty, locally grown food. It’s also a campaign to protect the world’s future food supply. Most people in the well-fed world give little thought to where their food comes from or how it’s grown. They wander through well-stocked supermarkets without realizing that there may be problem ahead. We’ve been hearing for some time about the loss of flora and fauna in our rainforests. Very little, by contrast, is being said or done about the parallel decline in the diversity of the foods we eat.

E Food variety extinction is happening all over the world - and it's happening fast. In the United States an estimated 90 percent of historic fruit and vegetable varieties are no longer grown. Of the 7,000 different apple varieties that were grown in the 1800s, fewer than a hundred remain. In the Philippines thousands of varieties of rice once thrived; now only about a hundred are grown there. In China 90 percent of the wheat varieties cultivated just a hundred years ago have disappeared. Experts estimate that in total we have lost more than 50 percent of the world's food varieties over the past century.

F Why is this a problem? Because if disease or future climate change affects one of the handful of plants we've come to depend on to feed our growing planet, we might desperately need one of those varieties we've let become extinct. The loss of the world's cereal diversity is a particular cause for concern. A fungus called Ug99, which was first identified in Uganda in 1999, is spreading across the world's wheat crops. From Uganda it moved to Kenya, Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen. By 2007 it had jumped the Persian Gulf into Iran. Scientists predict that the fungus will soon make its way into India and Pakistan, then spread to Russia and China, and eventually the USA.

G Roughly 90 percent of the world's wheat has no defense against this particular fungus. If it reached the USA, an estimated one billion dollars' worth of crops would be at risk. Scientists believe that in Asia and Africa alone, the portion currently in danger could leave one billion people without their primary food source. A famine with significant humanitarian consequences could follow, according to Rick Ward of Cornell University.

H The population of the world is expected to reach nine billion by 2045. Some experts say we'll need to double our food production to keep up with this growth. Given the added challenge of climate change and disease, it is becoming ever more urgent to find ways to increase food yield. The world has become increasingly dependent upon a technology-driven, one-size-fits-all approach to food supply. Yet the best hope for securing our food's future may depend on our ability to preserve the locally cultivated foods of the past.

questions.question: Heritage Farm is different from most other nearby farms.

analyses.content: 原文明确指出这个农场与周围典型的现代农田形成了“鲜明的对比（in stark contrast to）”，这意思就是它与附近的大多数农场都不一样。
你可能会因为不认识“in stark contrast to（截然不同）”这个词组而不敢选，其实只要看到“contrast（对比）”就能猜到两边是不一样的。
Everything about Heritage Farm is in stark contrast to the surrounding acres of intensively farmed fields of corn and soybean that are typical of modern agriculture.

questions.question: Most nongovernment-owned seed banks are bigger than Seed Savers Exchange.

analyses.content: 原文说它是美国最大的非政府种子库“之一（one of the largest）”，这直接推翻了题目说的“大多数（Most）都比它大”。
你可能会被题目里的比较级绕晕，只要看到原文写了“最大之一”，就说明没几个能比它大，绝对不可能有“大多数”比它大。
It is home to the Seed Savers Exchange, one of the largest non government-owned seed banks in the United States.

questions.question: Diane Ott Whealy's grandfather taught her a lot about seed varieties.

analyses.content: 原文只说了曾祖父把两种植物幼苗带到了美国并传给了她，但通篇没提曾祖父有没有“教过（taught）”她相关知识。
你可能一看到曾祖父留了种子给她，就自己脑补长辈肯定也教了她种地知识，做判断题最忌讳自己加戏。
In 1975 Diane Ott Whealy was given the seedlings of two plant varieties that her great grandfather had brought to America from Bavaria in 1870: Grandpa Ott’s morning glory and his German Pink tomato.

questions.question: The seeds people give to the Seed Savers Exchange are stored outdoors.

analyses.content: 原文说人们捐赠的种子存放在冷库、冷柜和地窖里（coolers, freezers, and root cellars），这些全是室内设施，直接证明题目说的“室外（outdoors）”是错的。
你可能会因为不认识“root cellars（地窖）”而卡住，但只要认识“freezers（冷柜）”就能知道，没人会把冷柜敞着门放在露天的室外。
The exchange now has more than 13,000 members, and the many thousands of heirloom varieties they have donated are kept in its walk-in coolers, freezers, and root cellars.

questions.question: Diane and her husband choose which heirloom seeds to grow on Heritage Farm.

analyses.content: 原文虽然提到了他们建立农场，并在那里种了各种蔬菜花草，但根本没说是他们自己去“挑选（choose）”要种哪些传家宝种子的。
你看到他们建了农场又种了植物，可能就会想当然地觉得植物品种也是他们自己挑的，千万别把没写出来的动作强加给作者。

Wanting to preserve similar traditional varieties, known as heirloom plants, Diane and her husband, Kent, decided to establish a place where the seeds of the past could be kept and traded. The exchange now has more than 13,000 members, and the many thousands of heirloom varieties they have donated are kept in its walk-in coolers, freezers, and root cellars. As you walk around an old red barn that is covered in Grandpa Ott’s beautiful morning glory blossoms, you come across the different vegetables, herbs, and flowers they have planted there.

questions.question: The seeds are listed in alphabetical order in The Seed Savers Exchange Yearbook.

analyses.content: 原文只说这本年鉴里一页又一页地列出了各种种子的名字和历史，但没提它们是不是按“字母顺序（alphabetical order）”排的。
你可能看到书像“电话簿（telephone directory）”一样厚，就联想到电话簿是按字母排的，这是用你的常识做题，而不是用原文做题。

“Each year our members list their seeds in this,” Diane Ott Whealy says, handing over a copy of the Seed Savers Exchange 2010 Yearbook. It is as thick as a big-city telephone directory, with page after page of exotic beans, garlic, potatoes, peppers, apples, pears, and plums—each with its own name and personal history.

questions.question: The Seed Savers Exchange Yearbook describes how each seed was obtained.

analyses.content: 原文提到每个种子都有它的“个人历史”，接着就举例说有的是俄罗斯老太太带来的、有的是集市上找的，这就完美对应了题目说的“描述了种子是怎么获得的（how each seed was obtained）”。
你可能会觉得“personal history”这词太笼统不敢判断，遇到这种抽象词，往下多读一句看看具体的例子，答案就一目了然了。

It is as thick as a big-city telephone directory, with page after page of exotic beans, garlic, potatoes, peppers, apples, pears, and plums—each with its own name and personal history. For example, there’s an Estonian Yellow Cherry tomato, which was brought to the seed bank by “an elderly Russian lady” who lived in Tallinn, and a Persian Star garlic from “a bazaar in Samarkand.” There’s also a bean donated by archaeologists searching for pygmy elephant fossils in New Mexico.

analyses.content: 原文写着超市偏爱那些为了好运输以及拥有统一外观（uniform appearance）而培育的品种，“uniform”正好同义替换题目的“standard（标准的、统一的）”，所以填 appearance。
你可能把注意力全放在前面的“ship well”上而忽略了后半句，顺着往后看，找准“uniform”这个替换词，答案就不难找了。

Found mostly in farmers' markets and boutique groceries, heirloom varieties have been squeezed out of supermarkets in favor of modern single-variety fruits and vegetables bred to ship well and have a uniform appearance, not to enhance flavor.
原文说人们常听说“热带雨林（rainforests）”里动植物的流失，但很少有人知道食物多样性的下降，这跟题目里的两面对比逻辑一模一样。
你可能不认识“flora and fauna（动植物）”，但这不重要，抓住“loss（对应disappearing）”这个动作，它发生在哪里，就填哪个地点。
We’ve been hearing for some time about the loss of flora and fauna in our rainforests. Very little, by contrast, is being said or done about the parallel decline in the diversity of the foods we eat.
原文明确写着过去种的几千种“苹果（apple）”里，现在剩下的不到一百种（fewer than a hundred），完全对应题目的“less than 100”。
你可能一看到第21句的“90 percent”就急着找词填，一定要记住用题目里的具体线索“less than 100”去精准定位，别被前面无关的数字带跑。
Of the 7,000 different apple varieties that were grown in the 1800s, fewer than a hundred remain.
原文说在过去一个世纪里，世界食物品种已经流失了超过“50 percent”，直接照抄这个百分比填进空里就行。
你可能看到原文的“more than”就想把它一起填进去，但题目空前已经给你“over”了，再填就是意思重复，填空题一定要看清空前给的词。
Experts estimate that in total we have lost more than 50 percent of the world's food varieties over the past century.
原文提到亚非地区的这种危险情况可能随之引发一场“饥荒（famine）”，这个“follow（随之发生）”正好对应题目中的“lead to（导致）”。
你可能想去填后面的“humanitarian consequences”，但留意题目空格前面有个“a”，这说明你只能填一个单数可数名词，所以只能填 famine。

Scientists believe that in Asia and Africa alone, the portion currently in danger could leave one billion people without their primary food source. A famine with significant humanitarian consequences could follow, according to Rick Ward of Cornell University.
原文说我们需要让食物产量翻倍来应对“这种增长（this growth）”，往前看一句，发现说的正是世界“人口（population）”将达到90亿的增长，所以填 population。
你可能一看到38句的“double”就只盯着这一句找答案，做题时如果遇到“this”这种指代词，一定要往回看一句才知道它到底在指代什么。
The population of the world is expected to reach nine billion by 2045. Some experts say we'll need to double our food production to keep up with this growth.
